name: Little Bighorn Battlefield National Monument
author: author-E-2026-10-18
summary:
Little Bighorn Battlefield National Monument is 765 acres of ridgelines, coulees and native prairie above the Little Bighorn River in southeastern Montana, in two parcels inside the exterior boundaries of the Crow Indian Reservation. On June 25 and 26, 1876, twelve companies of the 7th U.S. Cavalry under Lt. Col. George Armstrong Custer, with Arikara and Crow scouts, fought allied Lakota, Cheyenne and Arapaho people camped along the river under the spiritual leadership of Tatanka-Iyotanka (Sitting Bull). Lakota and Cheyenne warriors defeated the regiment. Custer and every member of his immediate command, about 210 men, were killed, and another 53 died in the companies under Maj. Marcus Reno and Capt. Frederick Benteen. [1] [2]

The NPS brochure traces the battle to the 1868 Fort Laramie treaty: gold was found in the Black Hills, the heart of the reservation, in 1874, thousands of gold seekers swarmed in in violation of the treaty, and in December 1875 the commissioner of Indian Affairs ordered the tribes to return before January 31, 1876, or be treated as hostiles. The Indians won the battle, the brochure says, but subsequently lost the war against the military’s efforts to end their independent, nomadic way of life. The park’s 2015 foundation document says the outcome shocked the nation and heightened threats to the cultural survival of all Indian peoples. [1] [2]

The battlefield was established as a national cemetery in 1879, and in 1890 the Army set 249 headstone markers where Custer’s men fell. In 1991 Congress renamed Custer Battlefield National Monument as Little Bighorn Battlefield National Monument and authorized a memorial to the Indian participants; since 1999 the Park Service has placed red granite markers at known Cheyenne and Lakota warrior casualty sites. The foundation document calls it sacred ground, contested ground and shared ground. [1] [2]

indigenous.html:
The 2003 Indian Memorial dedication program counts about 7,000 Sioux, Cheyenne and Arapaho people camped in the valley of the Greasy Grass, and 35 Arikara and six Crow scouts riding with Custer. The program adds that Arikara scouts killed in the valley fight, among them Bloody Knife, were buried where they fell and later reburied with the cavalry dead in the mass grave at Last Stand Hill, and that Sioux and Cheyenne relatives placed stone cairns where their people had been killed or wounded. [1]

In 1988, protesting the lack of an Indian memorial, American Indian Movement members cemented a plaque near the cavalry’s mass grave. The 1991 law authorized one, and it was dedicated on June 25, 2003, under the theme “Peace Through Unity,” identified by Cheyenne elder Austin Two Moons and Oglala Lakota elder Enos Poor Bear Sr. The Crow’s rights to the battlefield land passed to the United States in 1930. [1] [2]

women.html:
The park’s 2015 foundation document credits Elizabeth Bacon Custer’s efforts to enshrine her husband’s memory, along with the battle’s famous personalities, with profoundly shaping how film, theatre, art and literature portrayed it; in 1939 Congress authorized a museum and accepted her collection. [1]

In 1925 Nellie Beaverheart, daughter of the Cheyenne Lame White Man, who was killed in the battle, wrote to the War Department asking for a marker where her father died and was buried. The Army never responded. The Park Service placed a wooden marker for him on Battle Ridge in 1956 and replaced it with red granite on June 25, 1999. [1]

facts.claim: 765 acres in two parcels within the exterior boundaries of the Crow Indian Reservation, southeast Montana; northern parcel Custer Battlefield, southern Reno-Benteen; landscape features include ridgelines, coulees, ravines, native prairie, Little Bighorn River

facts.claim: Battle fought June 25 and 26, 1876, between 12 companies of the 7th US Cavalry under Custer, including Arikara and Crow scouts, and allied Lakota Sioux, Cheyennes and Arapahos under the spiritual leadership of Tatanka-Iyotanka (Sitting Bull)
facts.locator: Brief Description of the Park, p. 3
